title: ICSE CLASS 10 — Chemistry | Preparation of Salts
description: Subject-wise test on Preparation of Salts (Chemistry) for ICSE CLASS 10. 40Q.
subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following salts is prepared by the direct combination of its constituent elements?

options.explanation: Sodium chloride is prepared directly by the reaction of sodium and chlorine.
Copper(II) sulphate is prepared by neutralization or precipitation, not direct combination.
Lead(II) nitrate is prepared by reacting lead oxide with nitric acid, not direct combination.
Zinc carbonate is prepared by precipitation, not direct combination.

questions.explanation: Sodium chloride is prepared by burning sodium in chlorine gas (2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl), a direct combination method. Other salts are prepared indirectly by neutralization or precipitation.
questions.hint: Identify the salt formed by a direct reaction between a metal and a non-metal.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: The salt formed when dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with calcium carbonate is:

options.explanation: Calcium chloride is the salt formed in this reaction.
Calcium oxide is a base, not formed in this reaction.
Calcium hydroxide is a base, not formed in this reaction.
Calcium sulphate is not formed in this reaction.

questions.explanation: The reaction CaCO₃ + 2HCl → CaCl₂ + CO₂ + H₂O produces calcium chloride as the salt.
questions.hint: Recall the products of an acid-carbonate reaction.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which salt is prepared by the action of a dilute acid on a metal?

options.explanation: Copper(II) sulphate is prepared by reacting copper oxide with sulphuric acid, not directly with metal.
Zinc sulphate is prepared by reacting zinc metal with dilute sulphuric acid.
Sodium nitrate is prepared by neutralization, not by direct reaction of sodium metal with acid.
Potassium chloride is prepared by neutralization, not by direct reaction of potassium metal with acid.

questions.explanation: Zinc sulphate is prepared by reacting zinc with dilute sulphuric acid: Zn + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂.
questions.hint: Look for a salt formed by a metal reacting directly with an acid.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Assertion (A): The salt magnesium sulphate can be prepared by the action of dilute sulphuric acid on magnesium oxide. Reason (R): Magnesium oxide is a basic oxide and reacts with acids to form salts and water.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true, but the reason is the correct explanation for the assertion.

options.text: A is true but R is false
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true.

options.text: A is false but R is true
options.explanation: The assertion is true, and the reason is also true.

questions.explanation: MgO + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂O. The reaction is correct and R correctly explains why it forms a salt.
questions.hint: Evaluate both the assertion and reason for their validity and the reason's correctness.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: A student adds solid sodium carbonate to dilute hydrochloric acid. The salt formed and one of the by-products are:

options.explanation: Water is a by-product, but carbon dioxide is also produced.
Sodium chloride is the salt, and carbon dioxide is a gaseous by-product.
Sodium hydroxide is not formed in this reaction.
Sodium hydroxide is not formed in this reaction.

questions.explanation: Na₂CO₃ + 2HCl → 2NaCl + CO₂ + H₂O. The salt is sodium chloride and the gaseous by-product is carbon dioxide.
questions.hint: Recall the products of a carbonate-acid reaction.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: When a metal reacts with a dilute acid, a salt and hydrogen gas are produced. Which of the following metals will NOT produce hydrogen gas with dilute hydrochloric acid?

options.explanation: Magnesium reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas.
Zinc reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas.
Copper does not react with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas.
Iron reacts with dilute hydrochloric acid to produce hydrogen gas.

questions.explanation: Copper lies below hydrogen in the reactivity series and does not displace hydrogen from acids.
questions.hint: Identify the metal that does not react with dilute acids to produce hydrogen gas.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which salt is most likely formed if the metal carbonate used is calcium carbonate and the acid is dilute nitric acid?

options.explanation: Calcium chloride is formed from hydrochloric acid, not nitric acid.
Calcium nitrate is formed when calcium carbonate reacts with dilute nitric acid.
Calcium sulphate is formed from sulphuric acid, not nitric acid.
Calcium phosphate is not formed in this reaction.

questions.explanation: CaCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Ca(NO₃)₂ + CO₂ + H₂O. The salt formed is calcium nitrate.
questions.hint: Use the general reaction of a carbonate with dilute nitric acid to identify the salt.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which method is suitable for preparing potassium chloride from potassium hydroxide?

options.explanation: Direct combination involves reacting a metal with a non-metal, not suitable here.
Oxidation is not the method used to prepare potassium chloride from potassium hydroxide.
Neutralization involves reacting a base (KOH) with an acid (HCl) to form a salt (KCl).
Precipitation involves mixing two solutions to form an insoluble salt, not applicable here.

questions.explanation: Potassium chloride is prepared by neutralizing potassium hydroxide (a base) with hydrochloric acid: KOH + HCl → KCl + H₂O.
questions.hint: Identify the method used to prepare a salt from a base and an acid.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: The salt is soluble in water and forms a white precipitate with barium chloride solution. The salt is:

options.explanation: Sodium sulphate does not form a white precipitate with barium chloride.
Potassium chloride does not form a precipitate with barium chloride.
Zinc sulphate reacts with barium chloride to form a white precipitate of barium sulphate.
Ammonium nitrate does not form a precipitate with barium chloride.

questions.explanation: Zinc sulphate (ZnSO₄) reacts with BaCl₂ to give a white precipitate of BaSO₄. ZnSO₄ + BaCl₂ → BaSO₄↓ + ZnCl₂.
questions.hint: Identify the salt that forms a white precipitate with barium chloride, indicating the presence of a sulphate ion.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: The salt X is most likely:

options.explanation: Sodium carbonate does not decompose on heating to form an oxide and carbon dioxide.
Copper(II) carbonate decomposes on heating to form copper(II) oxide and carbon dioxide.
Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating but forms calcium oxide, not a metal oxide in this context.
Ammonium carbonate decomposes on heating but forms ammonia, water, and carbon dioxide, not a solid oxide.

questions.explanation: Copper(II) carbonate (CuCO₃) decomposes on heating: CuCO₃ → CuO + CO₂. It is prepared by reacting CuCO₃ (metal carbonate) with dilute acid.
questions.hint: Identify the salt that decomposes on heating to form a solid oxide and carbon dioxide.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following salts is used in the laboratory preparation of nitric acid by heating with concentrated sulphuric acid?

options.explanation: Sodium chloride does not contain the nitrate ion and cannot be used to prepare nitric acid.
Potassium nitrate is the correct salt used in the laboratory preparation of nitric acid.
Ammonium chloride does not contain the nitrate ion and is not used for this purpose.
Calcium sulphate does not contain the nitrate ion and cannot be used to prepare nitric acid.

questions.explanation: Potassium nitrate (KNO₃) is used in the laboratory preparation of nitric acid (HNO₃) by heating it with concentrated sulphuric acid (H₂SO₄): KNO₃ + H₂SO₄ → KHSO₄ + HNO₃.
questions.hint: Think of salts containing the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) that can decompose to form nitric acid.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: When a solution of sodium carbonate is added to a solution of calcium chloride, the precipitate formed is:

options.explanation: Sodium chloride is soluble in water and does not form a precipitate.
Calcium carbonate is the insoluble white precipitate formed in this reaction.
Calcium carbonate is the insoluble white precipitate formed in this reaction.
Sodium hydroxide is soluble in water and does not form a precipitate.

questions.explanation: The reaction between sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) and calcium chloride (CaCl₂) produces calcium carbonate (CaCO₃), an insoluble white precipitate: Na₂CO₃ + CaCl₂ → CaCO₃↓ + 2NaCl.
questions.hint: Look for the formation of an insoluble salt when two solutions are mixed.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: The salt used in the preparation of baking powder is:

options.explanation: Sodium sulphate is not used in baking powder.
Sodium bicarbonate is the correct salt used in baking powder.
Potassium chloride is not used in baking powder.
Magnesium sulphate is not used in baking powder.

questions.explanation: Sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃) is a key component of baking powder, which releases CO₂ when heated or mixed with acids, causing dough to rise.
questions.hint: Baking powder contains a compound that releases carbon dioxide gas when heated or mixed with moisture.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Assertion (A): Copper sulphate crystals are blue in colour due to the presence of water of crystallisation. Reason (R): The formula of copper sulphate crystals is CuSO₄·5H₂O.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
options.explanation: (R) is true, but it does not fully explain why copper sulphate crystals are blue.

options.text: Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
options.explanation: Both statements are true, but (R) does not correctly explain (A).
(R) is also true.
(A) is also true.

questions.explanation: The blue colour of copper sulphate crystals is due to the presence of water of crystallisation (CuSO₄·5H₂O), but the assertion does not specify the formula, making (R) an incomplete explanation.
questions.hint: Consider the role of water of crystallisation in determining the colour of copper sulphate crystals.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following salts is prepared by the direct combination of its constituent elements?

options.explanation: Sodium chloride is typically prepared by the reaction of sodium hydroxide with hydrochloric acid.
Iron(II) sulphide is prepared by the direct combination of iron and sulphur.
Potassium nitrate is prepared by the reaction of potassium hydroxide with nitric acid.
Calcium carbonate is prepared by the reaction of calcium hydroxide with carbon dioxide.

questions.explanation: Iron(II) sulphide (FeS) is prepared by heating iron and sulphur directly: Fe + S → FeS. This is a direct combination reaction.
questions.hint: Look for a salt formed by the direct reaction of two elements without involving other compounds.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: When a solution of barium chloride is added to a solution of sodium sulphate, the precipitate formed is:

options.explanation: Barium sulphate is the insoluble white precipitate formed in this reaction.
Barium sulphate is the insoluble white precipitate formed in this reaction.
Sodium chloride is soluble in water and does not form a precipitate.
Hydrochloric acid is a solution and does not form a precipitate.

questions.explanation: The reaction between barium chloride (BaCl₂) and sodium sulphate (Na₂SO₄) produces barium sulphate (BaSO₄), an insoluble white precipitate: BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓ + 2NaCl.
questions.hint: Look for the formation of an insoluble barium salt when two solutions are mixed.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: A student prepares a salt by reacting dilute sulphuric acid with zinc oxide. (i) The salt formed in this reaction is:

options.explanation: Zinc chloride is formed from the reaction of zinc with hydrochloric acid, not sulphuric acid.
Zinc sulphate is the correct salt formed in this reaction.
Zinc carbonate is formed from the reaction of zinc with carbonic acid, not sulphuric acid.
Zinc hydroxide is a base and does not form from the reaction of sulphuric acid with zinc oxide.

questions.explanation: The reaction is: ZnO + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O. The salt formed is zinc sulphate (ZnSO₄).
questions.hint: Consider the reaction between an acid and a metal oxide to form a salt and water.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: A student prepares a salt by reacting dilute sulphuric acid with zinc oxide. (ii) The type of reaction involved is:

options.explanation: Combination reactions involve two or more substances combining to form a single product.
Neutralisation reactions involve an acid reacting with a base to form salt and water.
Decomposition reactions involve a single compound breaking down into two or more simpler substances.
Displacement reactions involve a more reactive element displacing a less reactive element from its compound.

questions.explanation: The reaction is a neutralisation reaction as an acid (H₂SO₄) reacts with a base (ZnO) to form salt and water.
questions.hint: Consider the nature of the reactants and the products formed.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: A student prepares a salt by reacting dilute sulphuric acid with zinc oxide. (iii) The pH of the salt solution formed will be:

options.explanation: A salt formed from a strong acid and a weak base typically has a pH less than 7.
Zinc sulphate does not hydrolyse significantly, so the pH is approximately 7.
A salt formed from a weak acid and a strong base typically has a pH greater than 7.
The pH can be predicted based on the nature of the acid and base.

questions.explanation: Zinc sulphate is a salt of a weak base (ZnO) and strong acid (H₂SO₄), but it does not hydrolyse significantly, so the pH is approximately 7.
questions.hint: Consider the strength of the acid and base from which the salt is formed.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: The salt that is deliquescent and used as a drying agent is:

options.explanation: Washing soda (sodium carbonate) is not deliquescent.
Calcium chloride is deliquescent and used as a drying agent.
Potash alum is not deliquescent.
Blue vitriol (copper sulphate) is not deliquescent.

questions.explanation: Calcium chloride (CaCl₂) is highly deliquescent and is used as a drying agent due to its ability to absorb moisture from the air.
questions.hint: Look for a salt that absorbs moisture from the air and is used to dry other substances.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: A student adds a few drops of silver nitrate solution to a solution of salt X. A white precipitate is formed, which is soluble in dilute nitric acid but insoluble in ammonium hydroxide. The salt X is most likely:

options.explanation: Silver chloride is insoluble in ammonium hydroxide, but sodium chloride would not form a precipitate with silver nitrate.
Potassium chloride forms silver chloride, which matches the given properties.
Silver chloride is insoluble in ammonium hydroxide, but ammonium chloride would not form a precipitate with silver nitrate.
Silver bromide is insoluble in dilute nitric acid but soluble in ammonium hydroxide.

questions.explanation: The white precipitate is silver chloride (AgCl), which is soluble in dilute nitric acid but insoluble in ammonium hydroxide. The salt X is potassium chloride (KCl): KCl + AgNO₃ → AgCl↓ + KNO₃.
questions.hint: Consider the solubility rules for silver halides in different reagents.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: The salt used in the manufacture of glass and soap is:

options.explanation: Potassium nitrate is not used in the manufacture of glass and soap.
Sodium carbonate is the correct salt used in the manufacture of glass and soap.
Ammonium sulphate is not used in the manufacture of glass and soap.
Calcium chloride is not used in the manufacture of glass and soap.

questions.explanation: Sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃), also known as washing soda, is used in the manufacture of glass and soap due to its alkaline nature and ability to soften water.
questions.hint: Consider salts that are alkaline and used in industrial processes like glass and soap manufacturing.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a method of preparing salts?

options.explanation: This is a valid method for preparing salts, e.g., 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.

options.text: Reaction of a metal with an acid

options.text: Decomposition of a metal oxide by water
options.explanation: Metal oxides react with water to form bases, not salts.

options.text: Neutralization of a base with a non-metal
options.explanation: This is not a standard method; neutralization typically involves an acid and a base.

questions.explanation: Preparing salts by decomposition of a metal oxide by water is incorrect because metal oxides react with water to form bases, not salts.
questions.hint: Consider the products formed when metal oxides react with water.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: When dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with zinc granules, the salt formed is

options.explanation: Zinc oxide is not formed in this reaction.
Zinc hydroxide is not formed in this reaction.
The correct product of the reaction is zinc chloride.
Zinc carbonate is not formed in this reaction.

questions.explanation: The reaction is Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂, so the salt formed is zinc chloride.
questions.hint: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: A student adds a few drops of phenolphthalein to a solution of sodium hydroxide. The color observed is

options.explanation: Phenolphthalein does not turn red in a basic solution.
Phenolphthalein does not turn blue in a basic solution.
Phenolphthalein turns pink in basic solutions like sodium hydroxide.
Phenolphthalein is colorless in acidic solutions, not basic.

questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein turns pink in basic solutions like sodium hydroxide.
questions.hint: Recall the color change of phenolphthalein in acidic and basic solutions.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Assertion (A): Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) is an efflorescent salt. Reason (R): Efflorescent salts lose water molecules to the atmosphere on exposure.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.explanation: Both statements are true, and R correctly explains A.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.explanation: R is the correct explanation for A.

options.text: A is true, but R is false
options.explanation: Both A and R are true.

options.text: A is false, but R is true
options.explanation: A is true, and R is true.

questions.explanation: Washing soda is efflorescent because it loses water molecules to the air, and R correctly explains A.
questions.hint: Understand the definitions of efflorescent salts and the process of efflorescence.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which salt is prepared by the action of a metal on a dilute acid?

options.explanation: Calcium carbonate is not prepared by the action of a metal on a dilute acid.
Ammonium chloride is not prepared by the action of a metal on a dilute acid.
Magnesium reacts with dilute sulphuric acid to form magnesium sulphate.
Sodium nitrate is not prepared by the action of a metal on a dilute acid.

questions.explanation: Magnesium reacts with dilute sulphuric acid: Mg + H₂SO₄ → MgSO₄ + H₂, forming magnesium sulphate.
questions.hint: Consider the reaction between a metal and a dilute acid.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: A solution has a pH of 3. It turns blue litmus red and reacts with sodium carbonate to liberate a gas. The solution is most likely:

options.explanation: Sodium hydroxide is a base with a high pH.
Ammonium hydroxide is a base with a high pH.
Potassium chloride is a neutral salt with a pH of 7.
Sulphuric acid has a pH of 3, turns blue litmus red, and reacts with sodium carbonate to liberate CO₂.

questions.explanation: pH 3 indicates acidity; blue litmus turns red and reaction with Na₂CO₃ liberates CO₂ confirming acid (H₂SO₄ + Na₂CO₃ → Na₂SO₄ + CO₂ + H₂O).
questions.hint: Consider the properties of acids and their reactions.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following salts is prepared by the neutralization method using lead oxide?

options.explanation: Lead nitrate is prepared using lead metal or lead carbonate with nitric acid.
Lead oxide reacts with sulphuric acid to form lead sulphate.
Lead chloride is prepared using lead metal and hydrochloric acid.
Lead carbonate is prepared using lead nitrate and sodium carbonate.

questions.explanation: Lead oxide (PbO) reacts with sulphuric acid: PbO + H₂SO₄ → PbSO₄ + H₂O to form lead sulphate.
questions.hint: Consider the reaction between a metal oxide and an acid.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which salt is formed when copper carbonate reacts with dilute nitric acid?

options.explanation: Copper chloride is not formed in this reaction.
Copper oxide is not formed in this reaction.
The correct product of the reaction is copper nitrate.
Copper sulphate is not formed in this reaction.

questions.explanation: CuCO₃ + 2HNO₃ → Cu(NO₃)₂ + CO₂ + H₂O; the blue solution indicates copper nitrate formation.
questions.hint: Write the balanced chemical equation for the reaction.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: When barium chloride solution is mixed with sodium sulphate solution, the precipitate formed is:

options.explanation: Barium sulphate is the white precipitate formed.
This is a duplicate option and incorrect as per the explanation.
Barium carbonate is not formed in this reaction.
Sodium chloride remains in solution and does not form a precipitate.

questions.explanation: BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄↓ + 2NaCl; barium sulphate is the white precipitate formed.
questions.hint: Consider the solubility rules for precipitation reactions.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: What is the molar mass of HCl?

options.explanation: This is not the correct molar mass of HCl.
The molar mass of HCl is 36.5 g/mol.
This is a duplicate option and correct as per the explanation.
This is not the correct molar mass of HCl.

questions.explanation: Molar mass of HCl = 1 + 35.5 = 36.5 g/mol. The question asks for molar mass, not molarity. The molarity given confirms the calculation context.
questions.hint: Use the atomic masses of hydrogen and chlorine to calculate the molar mass.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following methods is **not** used for the preparation of a salt?

options.explanation: This is a valid method for preparing salts, e.g., 2Na + Cl₂ → 2NaCl.

options.text: Reaction of a metal with an acid
options.explanation: This is a standard method, e.g., Zn + 2HCl → ZnCl₂ + H₂.

options.text: Neutralization of an acid with a base
options.explanation: This is a common method, e.g., NaOH + HCl → NaCl + H₂O.
Sublimation is not a method for preparing salts; it is a purification technique.

questions.explanation: Sublimation is a physical process used to purify substances like iodine or ammonium chloride, but it is not a method for preparing salts. All other options (A, B, C) are standard methods for salt preparation.
questions.hint: Consider whether sublimation involves a chemical reaction.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following is the most likely pH at the end point of this titration?

options.explanation: This pH is too acidic for the endpoint of a strong acid-strong base titration.
This pH is still too acidic for the endpoint of a strong acid-strong base titration.
The equivalence point of a strong acid-strong base titration is at pH 7.
This pH is too basic for the endpoint of a strong acid-strong base titration.

questions.explanation: Phenolphthalein changes color in the pH range of 8.3–10.0. In a strong acid–strong base titration (e.g., NaOH + HCl), the pH at the equivalence point is 7. The color disappears when the solution becomes slightly acidic (pH < 8.3), so the most likely pH at the endpoint is 7.
questions.hint: Recall the pH range of phenolphthalein and the nature of the titration.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: **Assertion (A):** When lead nitrate solution is mixed with potassium iodide solution, a yellow precipitate of lead iodide is formed. **Reason (R):** Lead iodide is insoluble in water.

options.text: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
options.explanation: The assertion and reason are both correct, and the reason explains the assertion.

options.text: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
options.explanation: The reason correctly explains the assertion.

options.text: A is true, but R is false
options.explanation: Both the assertion and reason are true.

options.text: A is false, but R is true
options.explanation: The assertion is also true.

questions.explanation: Lead iodide (PbI₂) is indeed insoluble in water, forming a yellow precipitate. Therefore, both the assertion and reason are true, and the reason correctly explains the assertion.
questions.hint: Check the solubility of lead iodide in water.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the following salts will **not** produce an acidic solution when dissolved in water?

options.explanation: NH₄Cl produces an acidic solution due to the hydrolysis of NH₄⁺.
CuSO₄ produces an acidic solution due to the hydrolysis of Cu²⁺.
NaCl is a salt of a strong acid and a strong base, so it is neutral.
AlCl₃ produces an acidic solution due to the hydrolysis of Al³⁺.

questions.explanation: Sodium chloride (NaCl) is a salt of a strong acid (HCl) and a strong base (NaOH), so it does not hydrolyze in water and forms a neutral solution (pH = 7). The other salts (NH₄Cl, CuSO₄, AlCl₃) produce acidic solutions due to hydrolysis of their cations.
questions.hint: Consider the nature of the acid and base from which the salt is derived.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: What is the balanced chemical equation for the reaction of zinc oxide with dilute sulfuric acid?

options.explanation: This equation is incorrect because hydrogen gas (H₂) is not a product of this reaction.
This equation is incorrect due to the wrong formula for zinc sulfate (ZnSO₄).
This is the correct balanced equation for the reaction.
This equation is incorrect because zinc sulfite (ZnSO₃) is not formed.

questions.explanation: Zinc oxide (a basic oxide) reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form zinc sulfate and water. The correct balanced equation is ZnO + H₂SO₄ → ZnSO₄ + H₂O.
questions.hint: Write the products of the reaction and balance the equation.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: What is the correct observation during step 1 of the experiment to prepare copper(II) sulfate crystals?

options.text: The solution turns blue, and effervescence occurs
options.explanation: Effervescence (gas evolution) does not occur in this reaction.

options.text: The solution turns blue, and no effervescence occurs
options.explanation: The solution turns blue due to the formation of CuSO₄, and no gas is evolved.

options.text: The solution remains colorless, and a brown precipitate forms
options.explanation: The solution turns blue, not colorless.

options.text: The solution turns green, and a gas is evolved
options.explanation: The solution turns blue, not green, and no gas is evolved.

questions.explanation: Copper(II) oxide (black solid) reacts with dilute sulfuric acid to form copper(II) sulfate (blue solution) and water. No gas is evolved (no effervescence), so the correct observation is that the solution turns blue with no effervescence.
questions.hint: Observe the color change and whether any gas is evolved.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: What is the molarity of a sodium hydroxide solution prepared by dissolving 20 g of NaOH in 500 mL of water?

options.explanation: This would be the molarity if the volume were 1 L.
The molarity is calculated as 1.0 M.
This would require 40 g of NaOH in 500 mL.
This is not possible with the given data.

questions.explanation: Moles of NaOH = mass / molar mass = 20 g / 40 g/mol = 0.5 mol. Volume of solution = 500 mL = 0.5 L. Molarity = moles / volume = 0.5 mol / 0.5 L = 1.0 M.
questions.hint: Calculate the moles of NaOH and then divide by the volume in liters.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry

questions.question: Which of the given salts is deliquescent and commonly used as a drying agent?

options.explanation: Washing soda loses water (efflorescence), so it is not deliquescent.
Blue vitriol is a hydrated salt and does not absorb moisture to dissolve in it.
Quicklime reacts with water to form slaked lime but is not deliquescent.
Calcium chloride is highly deliquescent and used as a drying agent.

questions.explanation: Calcium chloride (CaCl₂) is highly deliquescent, absorbing moisture from the air and dissolving in it, making it useful as a drying agent. Washing soda (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) loses water (efflorescence), blue vitriol (CuSO₄·5H₂O) is a hydrated salt, and quicklime (CaO) reacts with water to form slaked lime but is not typically described as deliquescent.
questions.hint: Think about which salt absorbs moisture from the air and dissolves in it.
questions.subject: icse10-chemistry
